title: What a sacrament is
hookLine: an outward sign, given by Christ, that gives the grace it signifies (CCC 1131)

lines: SOME SIGNS DO WHAT THEY SAY.
cards: Most signs just point. A road sign says the bridge is ahead; it doesn't build the bridge. But a few signs do what they say.
A referee blows the whistle, and the game stops. A judge says you're married, and you are. Someone says I'm sorry, and something between you really shifts.
The words and the gesture don't just describe a thing; they make it happen. Catholics believe God works like that in seven particular moments of a life. Today, the word for them: sacrament.

teach.b: The word comes from Latin, sacramentum. In ancient Rome it meant an oath, the solemn vow a soldier swore when he joined the army, something that bound his whole life.
Early Latin Christians used it to translate mysterion, the Greek word behind the rosary's mysteries last week. So a sacrament is both: a promise that binds, and a mystery you can't fully see into.

The Catechism of the Catholic Church, in paragraph 1131, puts it this way: sacraments are signs that actually give grace, set up by Christ and entrusted to the Church, through which God's own life is shared with us.

teach.h: A SIGN THAT GIVES WHAT IT SHOWS.
teach.b: Older catechisms say it shorter: an outward sign that gives the grace it signifies. Water that washes. Oil that strengthens.
Bread that feeds. The sign isn't a picture of something happening elsewhere; Catholics believe it's where the thing happens.
And it doesn't depend on the priest being a saint that morning: the Church teaches that Christ is the one acting.
There are seven. Baptism, confirmation and the Eucharist bring you in. Reconciliation and the anointing of the sick heal.
Holy orders and matrimony set a life toward serving others. The Council of Trent confirmed the list of seven. Christians count differently here.
The Orthodox also speak of holy mysteries, and usually list the same seven. Lutheran and Reformed churches generally name two sacraments, baptism and the Lord's Supper.
Some communities, like the Quakers, keep no outward sacraments at all. Over the next week, i'll take the seven one at a time.

how: Catholics receive the seven sacraments at key moments of life, from baptism as a baby to anointing when seriously ill, with the Eucharist and confession received again and again.

o: a holy object kept and blessed in a church
a church ceremony that only symbolizes a belief
a sign Catholics believe really gives the grace it shows

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: the sacraments that bring you in

games.q: a road sign says bridge ahead. a referee's whistle stops the game. which is a sacrament more like?
o: the road sign: it points to something elsewhere.
the whistle: it makes what it signals happen.
games.why: Catholics believe a sacrament is a sign that does what it signifies, more like the whistle than the road sign.

practice: Look at your own hands and remember one time they did more than the motion: a handshake that closed a deal, a hand on a shoulder at a funeral, a ring put on a finger.
Recall it clearly, where you were and who was there, and see how a small outward thing carried something large. If you pray, give thanks for the signs in your life.

wordCard.voice: Sacrament. From the Latin for a soldier's oath: an outward sign, given by Christ, that Catholics believe gives the grace it shows. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: an oath or pledge, a soldier's vow. Latin Christians used it for the Greek mysterion.

carryVoice: Your line: signs that do something. Tomorrow, the first of the seven. See you then.
